speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Aloha, aloha, and welcome back to seven-eight-seven Flight Deck Notes. I'm Pualani — for the new folks, that's poo-ah-LAH-nee — and today we go holoholo through Flight Operations Manual Chapter 15. Security. Grab your coffee, buckle in the widebody, this one's got teeth.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] And I'm Chester, coming to you from a gray, drizzly Seattle morning — coffee in hand, condensation on the window, a seven-eight-seven line humming somewhere across the water, exactly how Boeing intended.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And I'm Otto. It's Chapter 15. It's long. It's the one chapter where the manual actually gets a little bit exciting. I've got the kettle on. Sweet as. Let's not muck about.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] The kettle. Otto, you cannot brew a cuppa mid-episode, this is a security chapter.

speaker: Otto
text: [deadpan] Watch me. Or don't. I'm the autopilot, Pua. I keep things level while you two flap about.

speaker: Chester
text: [laughs] The autopilot wants a hot beverage. Noted. Let's see if the eff oh em lets him have it.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Okay, Otto — since you're so level — set the table. Once we push back on the seven-eight-seven, who is actually in charge of security?

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Right. eff oh em 15.1.8. The Pilot-in-Command is designated as the In-Flight Security Coordinator — the ISC — for each flight. And here's the line to tattoo on your brain: once an aircraft door closes, security responsibility is transferred to the ISC.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] That's the handoff. On the ground before that, the Ground Security Coordinator — the GSC — owns it. The GSC reviews the security picture with the Captain before departure, and the moment that door thunks shut, it's the Captain's airplane and the Captain's security.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] I like a clean mnemonic for that. Ground before the door, ISC after. GSC hands to ISC. Say it with me next time you button up on the ramp at HNL: "Door closed, it's mine now."

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Poetry. Genuinely. Put it on a plaque next to the kettle.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] Pua, tell me about a time this actually clicked for you — like, the ISC thing stopped being a definition and became real.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Easy. Story a check airman told me, years back. Captain's out at the gate at HNL, GSC walks up, quiet, tells her there's a passenger who got into it with a gate agent — already de-escalated, but heads up. And fictional-Pua almost waves it off. But the check airman in the jumpseat goes, "That's your security picture. Log it in your brain. Because the second that door closes, that's your problem, not the GSC's." And that's 15.1.8 in one sentence. The handoff isn't a formality. It's the moment the buck moves to you.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And nobody hands the buck back. There's no receipt. You own it till the door opens again on the far end — Tokyo, Sydney, wherever the long night takes you.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] Speaking of the door. Can we talk about the door? Because this is the heart of the chapter, and honestly the heart of the airplane. eff oh em 15.2.6.1 — Secure Flight Deck. The Flight Deck Door shall be closed and locked from pushback — or engine start, if pushback isn't required — until the aircraft has been brought to a stop at its final position on the ramp and the engines are shut down.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Push to shutdown. The whole time.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And this is the big one for Rev 125, because the definition of a Secure Flight Deck changed. It is now a combination of a locked Flight Deck Door and, for aircraft so equipped, an Installed Physical Secondary Barrier — the I-P-S-B — between the cabin and the Flight Deck, for use when that door has to be opened.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And here is the line that matters. Any time the Flight Deck Door is opened during the Secure Flight Deck period, on an aircraft with the I-P-S-B installed, the I-P-S-B shall be deployed before the Flight Deck Door is opened. Before. Not while. Not after.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] Barrier first, door second. That is the whole rule in four words. Say it out loud on the walk to the airplane.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] And on the seven-eight-seven specifically — once the F-F-A or Flight Attendant is positioned in the Flight Deck entry way, the cabin observer deploys the I-P-S-B from the aft side of the barrier. Then the observer calls the Flight Deck to say the cabin is ready, and takes up a position by the first class bulkhead facing aft.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] And when the door is shut again, the "A" Flight Attendant stows the I-P-S-B. Deploy before, stow after. Also worth knowing which section you are in — 15.2.6.7 is Flight Deck Door Operations With I-P-S-B and it applies in flight. On the ground you follow 15.2.6.6, Flight Deck Operations Without I-P-S-B.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] So the same airplane, two different sections, depending on whether the wheels are turning. Tidy.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] The whole time. And 15.2.6.1 gives us the only reasons that door opens during that Secure Flight Deck period. There are four. A contamination check or em ee el inspection. To let a crewmember attend to physiological needs. To deliver or remove meal service items. And with the Captain's specific approval.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Four reasons. Not "I fancy stretching my legs." Not "the coffee's better up front." Not "I want to say gidday to my mate in row two." Four.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] Memory aid time — this is the first one I want everybody to circle. Think of it as the door's guest list, and it's short. Contamination check, physiological needs, meal service, Captain's approval. I run it as "Check, Comfort, Cart, Captain." Four C's, four reasons, straight out of 15.2.6.1.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Check, Comfort, Cart, Captain. That's clean. I'm stealing it. It's going on my kneeboard right under the drizzle stain.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] She's good at those. Credit where it's due. Annoyingly good.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Chur, Otto. I'll take annoyingly good.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And note the carve-out in the same section — Secure Flight Deck procedures are not required during Part 91 operations. Non-revenue positioning, that kind of thing. But scheduled passenger flying on the seven-eight-seven? Push to shutdown, locked.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Now, when that door does open — legitimately — how fast are we?

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] eff oh em 15.2.6.1. Crewmembers should strive to limit the time the door is open to three seconds or less. Three seconds. The manual literally says the Flight Deck is most vulnerable when the door is open, so you shrink that window as small as it goes.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] And still in 15.2.6.1 — if anyone perceives a threat while that door's open, any crewmember must loudly shout, quote, "Door, Door, Door," to alert the others to immediately close the Flight Deck Door.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] There's memory aid number two, and it writes itself — "Door, Door, Door." Three seconds, three doors. If you hear it, that door slams shut, no questions, no hesitation. It's the verbal fire alarm for the flight deck, straight from 15.2.6.6.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Otto, this feels like a "tell me about a time" one. You've flown the long Pacific legs. A door-discipline moment — one that stuck.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Yeah. HNL to Haneda. Fictional, mind you, but the flavor's real. Nine-plus hours across the Pacific, dead of night, jumpseater riding up front, First Officer wants a cuppa and a comfort stop. So we run the whole 15.2.6.7 dance, the With I-P-S-B one, because we are in flight — interphone the "A" Flight Attendant, she clears the forward galley and the lav, verifies no passenger disturbance, arranges the galley per Options 1, 2, or 3, the way the seven-eight-seven wants it. Cabin observer's got eyes aft. Door opens. And right then some bloke three rows back stands up fast, reaching into the overhead. Now — probably nothing. Probably his jumper. But the observer doesn't gamble on "probably." She shouts "Door, Door, Door," the door's shut before the eff oh's even got the kettle going. Turns out it was a jumper. Didn't matter.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Wait — so the eff oh never got the cuppa?

speaker: Otto
text: [deadpan] The eff oh never got the cuppa. Somewhere over the Pacific there is a cup of tea that was never made. I think about it often.

speaker: Chester
text: [laughs] The tragedy of Chapter 15. A perfectly good brew, lost to door discipline.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And you know what, though? Nobody's mad at you afterward for closing a door. That's the beautiful part. Worst case you re-run reentry. The point of the drill is you close first and sort it out through the cabin view port — or on the seven-eight-seven, the video surveillance system, not the other way round. You never lose money betting the door shut.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] That's it exactly. Three seconds, "Door, Door, Door," and the vulnerable window stays tiny. The tea is a small price.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Speaking of two people up front — eff oh em 15.2.6.7 — retitled in Rev 125 to Flight Deck Door Operations With I-P-S-B. Under Opening the Flight Deck Door With Crew Exit, a minimum of two people must be in the Flight Deck when the door is closed. So if a pilot steps out, someone backfills. If a pilot and a jumpseater both need to leave, the "A" Flight Attendant, or a designee, comes in to hold the number at two.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Never one. Two, always. It's the buddy system, but with a locked door and a lot more consequences than summer camp.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Chester, your turn — tell me about a time a jumpseater got handled right. The two-person rule done properly.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] So — Seattle, off-duty pilot in the jumpseat, and a brand-new First Officer, day two of IOE — Initial Operating Experience, for the folks not there yet. She's drinking from the firehose. Cruise settles down, the Captain needs to step out, and there's that jumpseater riding along. Green eff oh's brain goes, "Okay, I'm alone now, that's fine." But the second that jumpseater steps out too, you are not opening this door until the 'A' Flight Attendant is sitting in that seat." That's 15.2.6.7, cold. It's not about who's a pilot. It's about the number two.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Count the bodies. That's the whole rule in three words. Two bodies, door closed, every time.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] I love an IOE beat, because that's exactly where this stuff gets wired in — early, with someone watching, before the habits set. You learn the number two on day two, you've got it for a career.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And the note in 15.2.6.6 has a little gift — the Flight Attendant sitting up front to make the second-person count doesn't have to meet the flight-deck jumpseat facial hair policy. So the manual thought of that. Rare tenderness from a security chapter.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] The eff oh em, showing feelings. Screenshot it.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Hey Otto — did the jumpseater in that story ever get his cuppa?

text: [deadpan] Different flight, Chester. But no. There's a pattern forming. I'm beginning to think Chapter 15 is a conspiracy against hot beverages.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Now here's one people trip on — eff oh em 15.2.6.11. Medical personnel shall not be given access to the Flight Deck. Even a real medical event in the cabin. The door policy doesn't bend for it.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Right. And who does have access during Secure Flight Deck time? Back to 15.2.6.1 — it's limited to Alaska Airlines crewmembers, Federal Inspectors, Secret Service, Federal Air Marshals, and those with specific authorization. That's the list. Your onboard doctor, however heroic, is not on it.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Now the one that makes the hair stand up. eff oh em 15.2.6.3, Keypad Control. If the Flight Crew receives a keypad activation warning signal, they must assume — without any other information from the Flight Attendants — that a Level 4 Hijack or Attempted Hijack is in progress in the passenger cabin.

speaker: Pualani
text: [serious] No benefit of the doubt. That keypad tone is not "someone forgot the code." You assume the worst.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And 15.2.6.3 also says the keypad shall not be used for normal entry, and the crew denies keypad entry attempts. Normal reentry is the interphone-and-visual dance inside 15.2.6.6 and 15.2.6.7 — note 15.2.6.8 is now the freighter section, not the keypad. The pilots also confirm the switch position with each other so they don't inadvertently unlock the door.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] The keypad is the "break glass" option, and breaking the glass means hijack until proven otherwise. There's no "oops" reading of that tone. None.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Okay, let's get out to the checkpoint. Chester, kay see em.

Four S's means you go to the standard passenger checkpoint and get screened as directed.

text: [dry] Four S's, four letters, you're not special that day. Regular line for you, mate. Take your shoes off like a civilian.

text: [laughs] And 15.1.13.2 — you can't bring family, guests, or pets through kay see em or C-map either. It's you and your bags, that's it. No spouse, no dependents, no doggo.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So no, you cannot bring your own can of courage. Unless you're an eff eff dee oh, and that's a whole training pipeline, not a weekend hobby.

text: [serious] eff oh em 15.2.9.1. The FAM Team Lead provides their ID to the CSA and advises of additional team members. The CSA only needs to verify the Team Lead's ID. text: [warm] Pua, that's a "tell me about a time" if I ever heard one. The armed-LEO notification done right — you've got the HNL hub view.

text: [warm] Oh, I've got one. Fictional, but true to the ramp. HNL, boarding a long-haul. text: [dry] No surprises at ten thousand feet. That's the entire philosophy of 15.2.8 in one line. Before the door shuts, the map of who's armed is complete — and it's drawn in whispers, not on the radio.

text: [serious] That's the thing people miss — "handled right" doesn't look dramatic. It looks like nothing happened. Which is the goal.

text: [warm] Alright, passengers behaving badly. This is where a lot of the real-world stuff lives. The big one first, Chester.

text: [serious] eff oh em 15.3.5, Passenger Removal Procedures. There's a warning in all caps and it's the whole philosophy: NEVER take off with a KNOWN passenger disturbance.

text: [dry] Not "probably shouldn't." Not "use your judgment." Never. You sort it on the ground — at HNL, at Seattle, at ANC, wherever you're parked — where you've got police and a jet bridge, not a flight level and a problem.

text: [warm] And before you ever escalate against a passenger, there's a mindset check I really want people to keep — the "But For" test, eff oh em 15.3.1. You ask yourself: "But for this person's perceived race, ethnic heritage, or religious orientation, would I subject this individual to additional safety or security scrutiny?" If the answer is no, you stop, because the action may violate Civil Rights Law.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] That's a memory aid worth calling out on its own — the "But For" test. Two little words that keep your security decision anchored to behavior, not bias. Flight Attendants run it before notifying the Captain, and the Captain reviews it with them before acting. Straight out of 15.3.1.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Now the threat ladder. eff oh em 15.3.18 — there are four passenger threat levels. Level One, disruptive behavior, suspicious or threatening. Level Two, physically abusive behavior. Level Three, life-threatening behavior. Level Four, attempted breach of the Flight Deck or actual breach.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] One, two, three, four — disruptive, physical, life-threatening, breach. It climbs. Each rung is worse than the last.

text: [serious] And it ties straight into lockdown. eff oh em 15.3.13. And during Levels 3 and 4, the Flight Attendants will also lockdown the cabin.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] No circumstances. Level 3 or 4, the door is welded shut in your mind. text: [warm] Chester, this is where I always think of the movie line — the door stays closed.

text: [laughs] I mean, Maverick would want to open it and improvise. Top Gun. Feel the need, the need for speed. But the eff oh em is the exact opposite of hot-dogging it. Level 4, you feel the need to keep that door locked and get on the ground. No inverted flyby of the tower.

text: [warm] Okay, recap time. Otto, keep me honest. What's the spine of Chapter 15?

text: [excited] Which we remember as Check, Comfort, Cart, Captain. And when it's open — three seconds or less, and "Door, Door, Door" slams it shut, both from 15.2.6.1.
